analysis.one_liner: Makes losing plaintiffs automatically pay the winning side's legal fees in every federal civil case.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required federal courts to order any plaintiff who loses a civil lawsuit to pay the winning defendant's attorney fees — automatically, in every case, not just cases a judge deems frivolous. Businesses and insurers being sued would collect their legal bills from anyone who sues them and doesn't win. The bill was introduced on the first day of the 104th Congress, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Defendants — mainly businesses, insurers, and other repeat players in federal court — would gain a powerful new deterrent against being sued. Anyone thinking about bringing a civil rights, consumer, employment, or other federal claim would have to weigh paying the defendant's full legal bill if they lost, which would screen out weak and strong cases alike.

how_it_helps.text: A court must award a reasonable attorney's fee to any prevailing defendant in any federal civil action, automatically and without case-by-case judgment [S2] [S3].

The automatic fee award would fall on losing plaintiffs regardless of whether their lawsuit was actually frivolous; nothing in the bill requires a judge to find the suit groundless before shifting fees [S2] [S3].
For a defendant, even a meritless-seeming win would become profitable, since the losing plaintiff owes the defendant's legal costs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people and workers who sue — over civil rights, wages, discrimination, consumer protections, or injuries — would bear the risk of paying a company's attorney fees if they lose, and their lawyers would face pressure to turn down borderline but valid cases. Only defendants get fee awards under the bill; winning plaintiffs do not [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Plaintiffs who sue and lose, and their lawyers

drawbacks.text: The bill is one-sided: it shifts fees to losing plaintiffs only, not to losing defendants, so it tilts every lawsuit toward the party with more resources [S3].

Because the fee award is mandatory in every case rather than limited to suits a judge finds frivolous, a person with a real legal claim who loses on a technicality or close question of law would still owe the defendant's attorney fees — a bill many ordinary people could not afford [S2] [S3].
Automatically charging losing plaintiffs their opponents' legal bills would discourage legitimate claims, not just meritless ones, shrinking ordinary people's access to federal court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Deterring genuinely frivolous lawsuits is a fair goal, but this bill does not target them. It mandates fee-shifting in every federal civil case, applies only against plaintiffs, and would make the cost of losing a lawsuit — even a close one — ruinous for an individual. The deterrence it creates falls as much on valid claims as on weak ones, so the cost to ordinary people's access to court outweighs the benefit of fewer weak suits.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee on day one, passed along to a subcommittee three weeks later, and nothing ever happened after that — no hearing, no vote, nothing for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob Livingston introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day, and on January 25, 1995, referred to the Subcommittee on Courts and Intellectual Property [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill attracted no cosponsors and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people's access to federal court was preserved, since no law now forces losing plaintiffs to pay corporate defendants' attorney fees. Defendants and insurers that would have gained that leverage did not get it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Court access preserved; defendants gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Bob Livingston
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 104th Congress; it attracted no cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough to produce votes or recorded opposition; with zero cosponsors and no floor action, the record shows only the sponsor's support.

industries.note: The bill would have let businesses, insurers, and other sued entities collect attorney fees from anyone who sued them and lost. The bill died, so this advantage never materialized.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' attorneys and civil rights lawyers
industries.note: Mandatory fee-shifting against losing plaintiffs would have made lawyers cautious about taking borderline cases, shrinking the contingency-fee bar's caseload. The bill's death removed that threat.
Insurers, frequent defendants in litigation, would have gained a new tool to deter and settle claims cheaply. The bill never became law, so they gained nothing.
